From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 4: Seal of the Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Seal_of_the_Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation.svg/250px-Seal_of_the_Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Seal_of_the_Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation.svg)

The **FBI's Ten Most Wanted Fugitives during the 2000s** is a list, maintained for a sixth decade, of the [Ten Most Wanted Fugitives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives "FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitives") of the United States [Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation"). At any given time, the FBI is actively searching for 12,000 fugitives. During the 2000s, 36 new fugitives were added to the list. By the close of the decade a total of 494 fugitives had been listed on the Top Ten list, of whom 463 have been captured or located.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s#cite_note-Mueller-1)

## FBI headlines in the 2000s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: FBI headlines in the 2000s")]

The 2000s (decade) started out badly for the FBI's much needed attempts to upgrade technology. First, the "Trilogy" project went far over the $380 million budget, and behind its three-year schedule. Then, [Virtual Case File](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_Case_File "Virtual Case File") (VCF) planned for completion in 2003, was officially abandoned in 2005, after more than $100 million spent.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s#cite_note-2) A new, more ambitious investigation software project, Sentinel, was introduced in 2005 as a replacement for the failed VCF system.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s#cite_note-3)

In 2001, [Robert Hanssen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hanssen "Robert Hanssen"), high within the Bureau, was caught selling information to the [Russians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"), and Bureau security practices came into question.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI_Ten_Most_Wanted_Fugitives,_2000s#cite_note-4)

In 2002 the FBI's official top priority became [counter-terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter-terrorism "Counter-terrorism"), followed second by counterintelligence. The [USA PATRIOT Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USA_PATRIOT_Act "USA PATRIOT Act") granted the FBI increased monitoring powers.
